record_reviews.summary: Darwin rejects an inaccurate engraving of an ocellus, compares the cut with the marked feather, asks for Pearson and the engraver to correct the separate black-ring portions, and asks about the recipient’s health.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 4 April 1874], XML 1809-01-01 through 1874-04-03. The proof/engraving context is later than 1850.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes; the feather and engraving are physical objects referenced in the body, not surviving prose.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This answers an engraver/drawing exchange with no packet antecedent; the requested correction cannot be linked to a period source.

record_reviews.summary: Dunbar-Brander disputes Darwin’s explanations of dogs scratching after voiding and turning before lying down, offers a terrier case as evidence, and adds an observation that hares cry to their young.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 9 July 1873], XML 1809-01-01 through 1873-07-08. The explicit reference to Darwin’s book and St John’s work gives later context.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: J. B. Dunbar-Brander writes; the terrier and hare observations are his firsthand reports.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The letter answers Darwin’s published claims, but no packet prompt or contemporaneous reply is available.

record_reviews.summary: Breitenbach reports collecting insects and plants in Porto Alegre, plans to visit Fritz Müller after flood damage at Blumenau, describes mimicry and popular articles on evolution, mentions work on butterfly proboscides, and offers future reports.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 20 June 1881], XML 1809-01-01 through 1881-06-19. References to recent Brazil residence, Kosmos and later works place this outside the target period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Wilhelm Breitenbach writes in German; Fritz Müller, H. Müller, Ihering and von Koseritz are reported third parties.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The offer to send future observations is prospective; no Darwin prompt or received answer is in the packet.

record_reviews.summary: The surviving invitation names the Prince of Wales and asks Mr and Mrs Pender to request Darwin’s company on Thursday 23 June at 10 o’clock; it is a formal social fragment.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 23 June 1870], XML 1809-01-01 through 1870-06-22. The printed invitation date is later than 1850.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: The Pender invitation is an external printed/documentary voice; Darwin is only the invitee.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No correspondence prompt or reply survives; the invitation cannot support a Darwin-period link.

record_reviews.summary: Bronn asks whether a new English Origin edition or Darwin’s planned larger work is forthcoming, weighs positive and negative German reviews, defends natural selection as the only natural solution, and thanks Darwin for the Primula essay.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 11 March 1862], XML 1809-01-01 through 1862-03-10. The German edition and Primula reference provide later context, not period eligibility.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: H. G. Bronn writes in German; the separate scholarly annotations contain editorial material and were not folded into Bronn’s voice.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Bronn’s request answers a missing Darwin publication update and acknowledges a sent essay, but the input and physical receipt date are unavailable.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin gives a detailed list of engraved plates and wood-cuts to retain or correct, specifies figures, lettering and block groupings, and provides return addresses at Down and Queen Anne Street.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 30 June 1869], XML 1809-01-01 through 1869-06-29. The material is later than the target period on the available bound.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin is the writer; the plates and pencil instructions are production materials, not another correspondent’s prose.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The instructions respond to an engraver/proof exchange that is not included; no period prompt is available.

record_reviews.summary: The surviving list records plants common to Europe in Meyer’s Drége Cape collection, marks likely naturalisations, aquatic or marsh and seaside plants, and highlights unmarked cases of specific identity.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 9 May 1856], XML 1809-01-01 through 1856-05-08. The catalogue/list form and broad bound do not establish 1847–1850 composition.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: The list is attributed to Darwin’s exchange with Bunbury only through the header/apparatus; it contains cited Meyer/Drége material rather than a complete letter.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No question, acknowledgement or receipt is preserved; the list cannot support a specific link.

record_reviews.summary: Mary Butler asks Darwin to help find employment for Mr Thom, a capable newspaper manager whose health requires emigration to Queensland, and reports that Mr Smyth has obtained a Trinidad appointment; she closes with family news.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 25 December 1862], XML 1809-01-01 through 1862-12-24. No lower bound supports 1847–1850.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Mary Butler writes; Thom and Smyth are reported third parties, not correspondents.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The employment appeal is a direct request but no prior Darwin prompt or answer is in the packet.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin returns proof sheets, requests revisions and says he cannot complete six pages for a week or two; he comments on Mr Walker’s work and signs from Upper Gower Street on Friday.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [after 30 June 1839], XML 1839-07-01 through 1882-12-31. This open-ended range includes many years, including the requested period, but supplies no discriminating lower/upper date for 1847–1850.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes; the proof sheets and Walker’s work are missing surrounding context.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: An answer to Green’s enquiry is suggested by “You enquire,” but the prompt and receipt timing are not in the surviving source.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin acknowledges a reference, then answers a detailed argument about sexual selection: variability, sex differences, display, stridulating organs and spiders, closing with his own Beagle spider collection.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 20 February 1874], XML 1809-01-01 through 1874-02-19. The body’s reference to a prior letter and sexual-selection discussion are later than 1850.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes; Canestrini and other authors are cited external authorities, not the missing correspondent.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: A prior letter is explicitly acknowledged, but it is not in the packet and no date/receipt scope is recoverable.

record_reviews.summary: Julia Cameron sends a hurried answer about a respectable housekeeper and a gardener arrangement, while explaining the opening of a reading room and tenants’ plate and linen.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 10 July 1868], XML 1809-01-01 through 1868-07-09. The body’s “hurried answer” identifies a missing prior note but not a period date.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Julia Margaret Cameron writes; the household workers and reading-room logistics are third-party factual context.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The note answers an unlocated Darwin enquiry about domestic help; no source or receipt date permits a link.

record_reviews.summary: A writer asks the Duke of Argyll to read an enclosed memorial supporting Wallace and, if he agrees, inform Gladstone or permit that fact to be mentioned; the memorial will be signed by scientific men.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 27 December 1880], XML 1809-01-01 through 1880-12-26. The addressee is not Darwin and the source is far later than the period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: The surviving writer signs “Ch. D.” to a Duke; Darwin is not the voice or addressee despite the packet’s broad correspondence search.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This is a non-Darwin voice and cannot be used as a Darwin reply or period knowledge source.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin gives a long critical response to an unlocated book: Sprengel/Lubbock attribution, chlorophyll protection, cryptogam intercrossing, pleasure and pain, sexual selection, Hochberg, and Fritz Müller, ending by acknowledging safe receipt of the book.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 21 February 1879], XML 1809-01-01 through 1879-02-20. The book-review content and explicit receipt acknowledgement are later than 1850.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes; cited authors are external witnesses, and several phrases are bracketed/excised in the transcription.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The incoming book and its sender are not identified in the packet, so the response cannot be matched.

record_reviews.summary: Carus asks whether he may translate Darwin’s advertised book on interbreeding in plants, explains his Leipzig teaching schedule and hopes to visit, and requests an early answer.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 8 May 1873], XML 1809-01-01 through 1873-05-07. The advertised book and publication logistics are later than the period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: J. Victor Carus writes; the publisher’s request is reported third-party material.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The translation request is explicit, but Darwin’s incoming prompt/answer is absent and the date is outside the period.

record_reviews.summary: The surviving fragment says that the writer copied a passage from a life of Kepler and sent it to Darwin, receiving a handwritten thanks; the preserved text is Kepler’s religious passage about astronomy and divine wisdom.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 16 September 1880], XML 1809-01-01 through 1880-09-15. The broad later bound and fragmentary quotation do not establish period eligibility.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: The Kepler quotation is explicitly attributed and is not the sender’s own prose; Darwin’s alleged thank-you is reported but does not survive.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: A third-party quotation and reported Darwin response lack the original sender’s full source and receipt date.

record_reviews.summary: Frank Chance challenges Darwin’s beard-colour generalisation in Descent of Man with detailed self-observation, family inheritance claims, and enclosed hair/beard specimens, arguing for rare exceptions.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The header is [before 25 April 1871], XML 1809-01-01 through 1871-04-24. The explicit citation of Descent of Man places the exchange later than 1850.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Frank Chance writes; his own hair samples and family testimony are firsthand evidence, while Darwin’s published statement is quoted.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This is a response to Darwin’s book rather than a surviving period prompt; no receipt or answer is present.

issues: These are boundary_date_probe records. Broad before/after and alternative-year constraints were retained; packet membership was not treated as proof of 1847–1850 eligibility. Editorial bibliographies, scholarly sections, original quotations and preserved visual/enclosure material were read as apparatus or attributed evidence, not silently as Darwin voice.
